senses.sense_definition: The philosophical belief that life is meaningless and that all endeavours are devoid of objective purpose.

examples.text: Faced with personal tragedy, he struggled against a growing sense of <w>nihilism</w>.
The novel explores existential <w>nihilism</w> through the lives of disillusioned artists.

senses.sense_definition: The total rejection of moral principles, religious beliefs, or legal institutions.

examples.text: His complete disregard for ethical standards bordered on pure moral <w>nihilism</w>.
Critics accused the new political faction of preaching destructive social <w>nihilism</w>.

senses.sense_definition: A doctrine grounded on the negation of existence, asserting that nothing in the world truly exists or can be known.

examples.text: Ancient thinkers debated extreme forms of metaphysical <w>nihilism</w>.
Radical skepticism can eventually lead one into epistemological <w>nihilism</w>.

senses.sense_definition: A severe psychiatric delusion in which a person believes that they themselves, or the external world, no longer exist.

examples.text: The patient suffered from severe depression marked by persistent delusions of <w>nihilism</w>.
Clinicians observed signs of bodily <w>nihilism</w> during the psychiatric examination.

senses.sense_definition: Something that is completely devoid of value or meaning.

examples.text: Without meaningful engagement, those abstract rules were treated as mere <w>nihilisms</w>.
The author warned against reducing human achievements into historical <w>nihilisms</w>.

senses.sense_definition: The rejection of all unproven or non-rationalized claims in social and political spheres.

examples.text: Their strict rationalist approach resulted in political <w>nihilism</w> toward state dogmas.
The essay critiques modern forms of intellectual <w>nihilism</w> within academia.

senses.sense_definition: A revolutionary Russian movement of the 1860s that rejected traditional authority and advocated radical political change.

examples.text: Russian <w>Nihilism</w> challenged traditional authority and aristocratic traditions in the 1860s.
The tsarist regime viewed <w>Nihilism</w> as an existential threat to society.
